ap_physics_c_mechanics-f01.title: Block pushed by a force that grows with time

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=3\text{ kg}$ rests on a horizontal, frictionless surface. Starting at $t=0$, a horizontal force of magnitude $F(t)=ct$ pushes the block, where $c=3\text{ N/s}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the block, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the block while the force is applied. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Three arrows from the dot: weight straight down, normal force straight up with the same length, and the applied force horizontal in the direction of motion.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the weight (down), the normal force (up) and the applied force (horizontal), with no friction force and no force of motion
common_errors: adds a force of motion
draws a friction force on a frictionless surface

rubric_rows.criterion: The applied force arrow is horizontal and points in the direction in which the block accelerates
required_elements: horizontal arrow in the direction of motion
common_errors: draws the applied force at an angle

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight and the normal force arrows have the same length because the block has no vertical acceleration
required_elements: equal lengths of weight and normal force
common_errors: draws the normal force longer than the weight

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed $v(t)$ of the block as a function of time in terms of $m$, $c$ and $t$.
parts.model_answer: $a=F/m=ct/m$ and $v=\int_0^t a\,dt'=ct^2/(2m)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law to find the acceleration $a=ct/m$
common_errors: treats the acceleration as constant, $a=c/m$

rubric_rows.criterion: Integrates the acceleration with respect to time
common_errors: multiplies the acceleration by the time instead of integrating

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $v(t)=ct^2/(2m)$ using the initial condition $v(0)=0$
common_errors: omits the factor of one half

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the block at $t=3\text{ s}$ for $m=3\text{ kg}$ and $c=3\text{ N/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the values into the expression from part B
common_errors: uses the force at $t=T$ divided by the mass as the speed

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 4.50 with units of meters per second

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The experiment is repeated with a block of twice the mass. By what factor does the distance that the block travels during the first $3\text{ s}$ change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The distance is $x=\int v\,dt=ct^3/(6m)$, which is inversely proportional to the mass, so doubling the mass halves the distance ($x\approx4.50\text{ m}$ becomes $2.25\text{ m}$).

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the distance decreases by a factor of 2 (is halved)
common_errors: states the distance is unchanged
states the distance is divided by four

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $x=ct^3/(6m)$ or by noting that the acceleration at every time is halved when the mass is doubled
common_errors: argues only that heavier objects move less

ap_physics_c_mechanics-f02.title: Block-spring oscillator: graph, derivation and prediction

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=1\text{ kg}$ is attached to a horizontal ideal spring of spring constant $k=50\text{ N/m}$ on a frictionless surface. The block is pulled to $x=+A$, with $A=0.1\text{ m}$, and released from rest at $t=0$. Blank axes are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the position $x$ of the block as a function of time $t$ for two full oscillations. Label the amplitude and the period for the given values.
parts.model_answer: A cosine curve starting at $x=+0.1\text{ m}$ with period $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\approx 0.89\text{ s}$, repeated twice.

rubric_rows.criterion: The curve is a cosine: it starts at the maximum $x=+A$ at $t=0$
common_errors: starts at zero like a sine

rubric_rows.criterion: The amplitude is labeled or scaled as $0.1\text{ m}$ and the curve is symmetric about $x=0$
The period is marked as about $0.89\text{ s}$ and two full cycles are shown
common_errors: marks half of the period

rubric_rows.criterion: Both axes are labeled with quantities and units

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the maximum speed of the block in terms of $m$, $k$, and $A$ using conservation of energy.
parts.model_answer: $\tfrac12kA^2=\tfrac12mv_{max}^2$ so $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the energy at $x=A$ as only elastic: $E=\tfrac12kA^2$
common_errors: includes a kinetic energy term at the turning point

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets the energy equal to the kinetic energy at $x=0$: $\tfrac12kA^2=\tfrac12mv_{max}^2$
common_errors: uses $kA=mv$

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$
common_errors: omits the square root

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum speed and the magnitude of the maximum acceleration of the block.
parts.model_answer: $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}\approx 0.71\text{ m/s}$ and $a_{max}=kA/m\approx 5.00\text{ m/s}^2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the maximum speed of about 0.71 with units of meters per second
common_errors: leaves out the square root

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses Newton's second law at the turning point: $a_{max}=kA/m$
common_errors: uses $a_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the maximum acceleration of about 5.00 with units of meters per second squared

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The block is replaced by one with $9$ times the mass, released from the same position. Predict by what factor the period changes, and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The period increases by a factor of $\sqrt{9}=3$ ($T\approx2.67\text{ s}$), because $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the period increases by a factor of $3$
common_errors: states the period is unchanged
states a factor of 9

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ (the period is proportional to the square root of the mass)
common_errors: argues only that heavier blocks move more slowly

ap_physics_c_mechanics-f08.title: Bullet embedding in a pivoted rod

stimulus.description: A uniform rod of mass $M=3\text{ kg}$ and length $L=0.8\text{ m}$ hangs from a frictionless pivot at its upper end. A bullet of mass $m=50\text{ g}$ moving horizontally at $v=100\text{ m/s}$ strikes the lower end of the rod and embeds in it. The rotational inertia of the rod about the pivot is $\tfrac13ML^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that the total mechanical energy of the bullet and rod is conserved in the collision. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer by identifying a quantity that is conserved about the pivot.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The collision is perfectly inelastic, so mechanical energy is not conserved, but the angular momentum about the pivot is conserved because the force at the pivot has no torque about it.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees that the mechanical energy is conserved
common_errors: agrees that the energy is conserved

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by identifying the angular momentum about the pivot as the conserved quantity
required_elements: angular momentum about the pivot is conserved
common_errors: says the linear momentum is conserved

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that the pivot force exerts no torque about the pivot (or that external torques are zero during the collision)
required_elements: pivot force has zero torque about the pivot
common_errors: argues only that there are no external forces

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the angular speed $\omega$ of the rod and bullet just after the collision in terms of $m$, $v$, $M$ and $L$, and calculate its value.
parts.model_answer: $mvL=(\tfrac13ML^2+mL^2)\omega$ so $\omega=mvL/(\tfrac13ML^2+mL^2)\approx5.95\text{ rad/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the initial angular momentum of the bullet about the pivot, $mvL$
common_errors: uses $mv$ without the lever arm

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the final angular momentum $(\tfrac13ML^2+mL^2)\omega$ and solves for $\omega$
common_errors: omits the bullet from the final rotational inertia

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $\omega$ of about 5.95 with units of radians per second

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the fraction of the bullet's initial kinetic energy that remains as kinetic energy of the rod and bullet just after the collision.
parts.model_answer: The fraction is $\tfrac12I\omega^2/(\tfrac12mv^2)=mL^2/I\approx0.0476$ (almost all of the energy is dissipated).

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $K=\tfrac12I\omega^2$ for the final kinetic energy and $\tfrac12mv^2$ for the initial
common_errors: uses $K=\tfrac12m\omega^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains a fraction of about 0.048 (accept any value within 5 percent)
common_errors: uses the fraction of the angular momentum
